title: AI Music Generator Suno Strikes Licensing Deal With BMG as It Preps New Label-Backed Models
full_text: Aug 12, 2026 3:00am PT AI Music Generator Suno Strikes Licensing Deal With BMG as It Preps New Label-Backed Models By Corbin Bolies Plus Icon Corbin Bolies Latest AI Music Company Suno Unveils Download Caps for Free, Paid Tiers in Quest to Combat Abuse (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago Mark Zuckerberg Says He’s Surprised the ‘Discourse’ From AI Companies ‘Is So Filled With Doom’ 2 days ago Why Higgsfield Inked Deals for AI Avatars of Streamer N3on, UFC’s Israel Adesanya and Quinton ‘Rampage’ Jackson, and More for New Film (EXCLUSIVE) 7 days ago See All Courtesy of Suno Suno , the AI music generator that’s managed to both rankle the music industry and lure some of its biggest talent to its side, has added music company BMG as its latest licensing partner as it prepares new models powered by licensed work. The partnership will see Suno pay for BMG’s repertoire of recordings from its artists, while also covering the use of any BMG songs to train Suno’s past models. BMG joins Warner Music Group in settling with the music-generation company, which has been the target of a series of lawsuits alleging unauthorized use of audio recordings to train its data. Related Stories Rod Stewart Cancels Upcoming Tour Dates Following Coronary Stent Procedure ‘SNL U.K.’ Season 2 Sets September Date “We believe the future of music will be more participatory, creating entirely new ways for artists and fans to connect,” Suno CEO and co-founder Mikey Shulman said in a statement. “Building that future responsibly means working directly with the people who make music and the companies that represent them. Together with BMG, we can develop new experiences that give artists and songwriters real choice, generate new revenue, and make music a bigger part of people’s lives.” Popular on Variety Celine Joshua, BMG’s executive vice president of global marketing and streaming, framed music’s future as one where artists and songwriters “share in the value” platforms such as Suno may create. “Choice is the guiding principle,” Joshua said. “This agreement establishes strong protections, clear economics, and new creative possibilities for artists and their fans. As we enter the era of creation, we look forward to shaping that future together with our creators and Suno.” The settlement marks BMG’s most notable acceptance of AI’s role in music since the generative era began. It sued Anthropic in California federal court earlier this year for allegedly using its copyrighted works, including songs by the likes of Bruno Mars and the Rolling Stones, to train its models in what it called a scheme of “widespread and systematic infringement.” The case, similar to one brought by other music publishers in 2023, is ongoing. BMG also joined a collection of other music labels and companies last month, including WMG, Universal Music Group and Sony Music, in proposing a new set of guidelines for how AI-generated music could chart on music tracking lists, specifying that only tracks that were “substantially human made” qualify for the industry’s measure of success. The deal with BMG also gives Suno another layer of legitimacy as it prepares its new industry-backed models, which Suno said on Monday would come soon. Last week, Suno said it would begin watermarking songs downloaded from the platform to help signify the use of AI and limit song downloads for its three usage tiers to combat slop, efforts the company is taking to further legitimize its outputs among the music industry. Still, Suno is facing ongoing lawsuits from UMG and Sony Music for copyright infringement, and last month a German court found that the company was violating U.S. and German copyright laws. S.S. full_text: Aug 12, 2026 2:05am PT U.K.’s Largest Harry Potter Store Opening in London Ahead of HBO Series Launch By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest U.K.’s Largest Harry Potter Store Opening in London Ahead of HBO Series Launch 1 hour ago Jessica Reynolds and Charlotte Rampling to Star in Opera Drama ‘Maya Butterfly’ (EXCLUSIVE) 20 hours ago George MacKay, Louisa Harland, Nathalie Emmanuel and Eric Kofi Abrefa Join ‘The Animals’ From ‘Supacell’ Star Calvin Demba (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago See All HBO With Harry Potter excitement expected to reach fever pitch once more later this year with the launch of HBO’s new TV series, Warner Bros. is going big on the merch — and just in time for Christmas. The studio has announced that the U.K. largest Harry Potter shop will open in central London in November, weeks before the hotly-anticipated series premieres on Dec. 25. The flagship store, which will span two floors and more than 21,000 square-feet, will be located on the main shopping area of Oxford Street and has, according to Warner Bros., taken inspiration from the Wizarding World’s own magical shopping street Diagon Alley. It is set to feature a dragon towering above Gringotts bank, a full-sized Knight Bus and also a branch of the Leaky Cauldron pub serving food and foaming Butterbeer. Related Stories Tammy Fine to Lead Talent Development at NBC News 'The Daily Show' Releases Audition Tapes for John Oliver, Michael Che, Current Hosts and More “There’s no better place to create a destination that celebrates the magic, creativity and storytelling that has captivated generations of fans around the world,” said Karl Durrant, Warner Bros,’ senior vice-president of worldwide retail, in a statement, adding that the opening of the store was “a truly special milestone.” Popular on Variety The Oxford Street location will become the second official Harry Potter store in the U.K. after the site at King’s Cross Station, where Potter and his fellow young wizards famously catch the train to Hogwarts. But the new store will reportedly include various exclusives, including a Diagon Alley wand, a special Funko Pop and a MinaLima artwork inspired by the Knight Bus and Diagon Alley. Alongside the official shops, there are numerous other unofficial stores selling Potter-themed merchandise scattered around London city center and other tourist hotspots. Perhaps coincidentally (or perhaps a sign of a darker wizarding power in the commercial sector), less than a day before the news of the Oxford Street store was announced, one of these unofficial stores was reported to have closed down. title: AI-Generated Turkish Series ‘Castle Walls’ Launches on Prime Video in What Is Being Touted as a Worldwide Streaming First – Trailer (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Aug 12, 2026 2:01am PT AI-Generated Turkish Series ‘Castle Walls’ Launches on Prime Video in What Is Being Touted as a Worldwide Streaming First – Trailer (EXCLUSIVE) "Castle Walls" spans two 15-minute episodes and features a fortress that is popular as a location in Ubisoft’s “Assassin’s Creed Mirage” video game By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest RTL Group Posts 3.9% Revenue Rise as Streaming Side Grows 1 day ago Giovanni Tortorici on Working With Monica Bellucci Who Plays an ‘Eccentric’ Aristocratic Matron in His Luca Guadagnino-Produced Film ‘Ketticè’ 4 days ago Cinema Ritrovato Chief Gianluca Farinelli Appointed Artistic Director of Italy’s David di Donatello Awards 7 days ago See All Courtesy Ay Yapim AI-generated historical drama “Castle Walls,” produced by Turkish TV powerhouse Ay Yapim , is launching Wednesday on Prime Video in what is being touted as the first show made end-to-end using artificial intelligence to premiere on a major global streaming platform worldwide. “Castle Walls” (“Surlar” in Turkish) spans two 15-minute episodes and focuses on the enigmatic story of present-day Iran’s Alamut Castle. The fortress has been made popular as a location in Ubisoft’s popular “Assassin’s Creed Mirage” video game. The short series is written by Turkish television veterans Kerem Deren and Çisil Hazal Tenim (“El Turco”). It is produced by Ay Yapim under its new Singapore-based subsidiary, AI Yapim. Related Stories U.K.'s Largest Harry Potter Store Opening in London Ahead of HBO Series Launch 'In Flames' Director Zarrar Kahn Returns to Toronto With Gym-Incel Rom-Com 'The Lion Does Not Concern Himself,' Trailer Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE) “Castle Walls” was made end-to-end using AI “for prompt enhancement and creative development,” using “a proprietary AI storyboard system developed in-house by AI Yapım, and AYDNA, a video diffusion model developed by the AI Yapım team and trained exclusively on Ay Yapım’s own licensed content catalogue,” according to an Yapim statement. Popular on Variety “Unlike many AI productions that draw on datasets of uncertain provenance, every element of the AYDNA training pipeline was built on rights-managed material,” the company added. The series is dubbed in every language by real human voice artists. Significantly, “acting performances are not AI-generated,” the statement specified. In a previous statement – released when the groundbreaking series was announced in Oct. 2025 – Ay Yapim had revealed that the show was developed over the the course of a year, and produced end-to-end using a mix of AI technologies, including ChatGPT, “for prompt enhancement and creative refinement,” the statement said. Generative artificial intelligence program MidJourney was used “for visual exploration and inspiration,” it had added, while AI video generator Runway and the Google Nano Banana image generating and editing tool were employed “for character integration.” Additionally, Veo, Kling, ComfyUI and Topaz were used “for video generation and cinematic execution.” Runway and AI voice generator ElevenLabs where used for voice and dubbing “merging creativity with execution,” the Oct. 2025 statement had noted. “The production process itself tells its own story,” Ay Yapim said in its statement on Wed. “The first episode was built shot by shot using an inpainting technique that predates the current generation of image-generation tools — completed before now-ubiquitous models.” “By the second episode, more advanced generative AI technologies were integrated into the pipeline,” it added. “The hand-drawn character and location sketches created by the human team before AI processing began demonstrate the level of creative and craft input that underpins every scene. This is not a production that bypassed human skill; it is one that used AI to amplify it,” the statement went on to point out. Ay Yapim is best known for the International Emmy-winning “Endless Love,” “Fatmagul,” “Ezel” and “Forbidden Love,” among other global hit series. The prominent Turkish TV outfit underlined that the “Castle Walls” launch builds on AI Yapım’s “growing role in the global conversation about AI and storytelling.” AI Yapım leads WAIFF Turkey, the Turkish chapter of the World AI Film Festival (WAIFF), the international event dedicated to films created with artificial intelligence. They also serve as the AI production capability-building partner of the International Academy of Television Arts & Sciences (International Emmy Awards) education program. “‘Castle Walls’ is the clearest expression to date of the argument both forums made: that AI-produced long-form content is not a future possibility but a present fact,” the Ay Yapim statement claimed. Amazon MGM Studios in May annnounced they had greenlit three animated AI series for Prime Video: “Punky Duck” from Jorge R. Gutierrez (director of “The Book of Life”); “Love, Diana Music Hunters” from Albie Hecht, chief content officer at pocket.watch (and the former president of Nickelodeon who developed “SpongeBob SquarePants”); and “Cupcake & Friends” from BuzzFeed Studios. All three series will premiere on Prime Video but no dates have been set yet. S.S. title: Lee Daniels, Nadine Labaki, Marina Abramovic Win Liberatum Pioneer Awards (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All August 12, 2026 2:00am (R to L): Nadine Labaki, Lee Daniels, Marina Abramovic Marc Piasecki/FilmMagic, Aliah Anderson, Jamie McCarthy Empire creator Lee Daniels , Capernaum director Nadine Labaki , and avant-garde artist Marina Abramovic will be honored at this year’s Venice Film Festival with the 2026 Liberatum Pioneer Awards. The awards, presented by Pablo Ganguli’s Liberatum cultural diplomacy organization, recognize artists whose work “has challenged convention, broken down systemic barriers, expanded artistic boundaries, redefined the possibilities of their respective fields and promoted the importance of preserving human dignity.” The awards presentations will take place in Venice on Sept 6 and 7 as part of the inaugural Liberatum Art & Cinema, a new multidisciplinary programme staged to mark the cultural group’s twenty-fifth anniversary. Related Stories Movies Makeup Oscar Record Holder Recalls Turning Jim Carrey Into the Grinch, Transforming Jacko for 'Thriller' and Playing King Kong Movies Crunchyroll, Sony Nab Makoto Shinkai's Untitled Next Anime Film for Global Release Announcing this year’s winners on Wednesday, Liberatum said it was recognizing Daniels, director for the “bold, uncompromising filmmaking that has consistently brought subjects largely absent from mainstream American film and television into major public view, including Precious , The Butler and Empire .” Daniels’ focus on the depiction of “Black life, trauma, sexuality and family with candour, at scale and without dilution,” the group said, “has opened space within the industry for narratives previously considered commercially untenable. His selection reflects Liberatum’s recognition of filmmakers who have used popular form to carry unpopular truths.” Labaki is being recognised for her feature films, including Where Do We Go Now? (2011) and Capernaum (2018). Both premiered in Cannes, with the latter and winning the Jury Prize, en route to an Oscar nomination for best international feature. The Lebanese director, Liberatum said, “has carried stories from Lebanon and the wider Middle East to international audiences on their own terms” by combining “documentary rigour with narrative craft to address displacement, poverty and conflict without sentimentality.” The Pioneer honor for Serbian performance artist Abramović, famous for her landmark “The Artist Is Present” (2010) piece in which she sat silently at a table for more than 700 hours over nearly three months, inviting visitors to sit opposite her and maintain eye contact is in recognition for establishing “performance art as a discipline in its own right and expanded its vocabulary further than any of her contemporaries,” the group said. “Abramović’s practice has repeatedly used duration, presence and physical risk to examine the relationship between artist and audience, and her influence now extends well beyond performance art into the wider language of contemporary visual culture.” Abramović this year also has a major solo exhibition at Venice’s Gallerie dell’Accademia, the first living woman artist to receive the honor in the institution’s 250-plus year history. Previous winners of the Liberatum Pioneer Award include actor Angela Bassett, Brazilian anthropologist Ivete Sacramento, and actor Ellen Burstyn, who was honored at the Venice film festival in 2024 . title: Donald Trump Waging $10B Legal War Against BBC On Basis “Doctored” Documentary May Have Been Viewed 285 Times In America
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake ‘Saturday Night Live UK’ Season 2 Gets Premiere Date ‘The Office’ Star Lucy Davis Reveals She Has Incurable Cancer Ari Emanuel’s Mari Agrees Deal To Buy ATG, Owner Of Theater Venues Behind Shows Like ‘Harry Potter & The Cursed Child’ View All August 12, 2026 1:30am Donald Trump is suing the BBC over a 'Panorama' documentary. Getty Donald Trump ‘s lawyers have accused the BBC of a “brazen” attempt to interfere in the 2024 U.S. election on the basis that fewer than 300 Americans may have seen a documentary that misleadingly edited his January 6 speech. Trump is suing the BBC for defamation in Florida for $10 billion, and his amended complaint against the British broadcaster incorporates newly discovered evidence about the viewing figures for the Panorama film, Trump: A Second Chance? , which premiered days before the presidential election. Trump’s new complaint claims that the documentary — which was produced by October Films and spliced together two parts of Trump’s Capitol riots speech — was streamed on iPlayer by “hundreds of individuals” in the U.S., despite it being geoblocked in America. Related Stories News Kennedy Center Ordered To Pay Jazz Musician Chuck Redd More Than $250,000 In Legal Dispute Over His Opposition To Trump Renaming News BBC Joins Working Title's New TV Adaptation Of 'Jane Eyre' Starring Aimee Lou Wood But the evidence was not this emphatic. Watch on Deadline The lawsuit attributes the new information to a deposition of Richard Cooper, the BBC’s director of digital distribution. Cooper revealed that the Panorama film was successfully viewed 570,000 times on iPlayer, but only 0.05%, or 285, of these streams originated from IP addresses that could have been based in America. Some 34 streams appear to have originated from IP addresses that may have been based in Florida, where the case is being heard. During his interview under oath, Cooper was repeatedly clear with Trump’s lawyers that although the BBC’s data “might identify the IP address as being from the United States, that doesn’t necessarily mean to say it originated from the United States.” He added that the Florida IP streams were linked to an internet service provider associated with a cruise ship company. Cooper also qualified that the BBC’s viewing figures were for the “entire period that the documentary was available.” This is important because it is not clear if the 285 potential U.S. streams came in the days leading up to the election, when Trump claims that election meddling took place. The Panorama film was on iPlayer for around a year before being pulled by the BBC. The BBC is defending the lawsuit, but has admitted failings over the Panorama film. title: Oscar Nominee Barkhad Abdi, Jim Deddes Lead Teddy Cherim’s ‘Maalstroom’; First-Look Image Released (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Aug 12, 2026 12:00am PT Oscar Nominee Barkhad Abdi, Jim Deddes Lead Teddy Cherim’s ‘Maalstroom’; First-Look Image Released (EXCLUSIVE) By Leo Barraclough Plus Icon Leo Barraclough International Features Editor LeoBarraclough Latest Oscars: Lithuania Submits ‘How to Divorce During the War’ for International Feature Race (EXCLUSIVE) 21 hours ago Samuel Goldwyn Acquires North America Rights to WestEnd Films’ Holiday Comedy ‘Merry Christmas Aubrey Flint’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago Jeremy Irons, Keke Palmer, Regina Hall and More Attached to Projects Launching at Toronto Market 2 days ago See All Courtesy of Thijmen Doornik Jim Deddes , Tenzing Woing and Somali-American actor Barkhad Abdi , known for his Oscar-nominated role in “Captain Phillips,” lead the cast of “Maalstroom,” which has just wrapped. Variety has been given the first-look image. The Dutch-Belgian co-production was written and directed by Teddy Cherim , and produced by Marten van Warmerdam. In “Maalstroom,” a struggling barge skipper Jan takes on an urgent shipment of sand from Dunkirk to Rotterdam in a last attempt to save himself from financial ruin. Shortly after setting off, he discovers 11 refugees hidden in his cargo. As Jan races north along the canals, his unwanted passengers force him to confront a reality far removed from his own and to see life from a new perspective. Abdi plays Bahdoon, a role Cherim wrote with him in mind. Popular on Variety Abdi received Academy Award and Golden Globe nominations and won a BAFTA for his breakthrough performance in “Captain Phillips,” and has since appeared in films including “Good Time,” directed by Benny and Josh Safdie, and Denis Villeneuve’s “Blade Runner 2049.” The cast also includes Abdulaal Hussein, Hana Hussein, Anas Derow, Merhawi Kesete, Hiba Ali, Issa Musa, Sabine Berhe-Hagosse, Orwa Zaid, Hanna Mussie and Mohammed Terwis. Cherim said, “The subject matter is heavy, but the film is at times also light-footed. The humor in ‘Maalstroom’ comes from the situation on board the ship, which is inherently surreal. The way Europe deals with migrants is fundamentally bizarre: the contradictions, the bureaucracy, the fear, the denial. The film holds up a mirror to that absurdity.” Cherim previously directed series including “Joardy Seaon” and “Vakkenvullers.” In 2019, he was nominated for a Golden Calf for the boundary-pushing VR documentary “Meet the Soldier,” in which viewers experience an encounter through the eyes of two tribes in Uganda — a project that also contributed to real-life reconciliation between the tribes involved. Van Warmerdam said, “The longer we work on this film, the more relevant it becomes. ‘Maalstroom’ makes a story tangible and recognizable by giving a face to the fears on both sides, through characters who unwillingly make the same journey aboard the same ship. The story brings the migration issue back to a human scale and shows both the dilemmas and the compassion that arise when lives truly touch one another.” The film is produced by Graniet Film in the Netherlands, in co-production with Czar Film & TV in Belgium and Dutch public broadcaster NTR. It is supported by the Netherlands Film Fund, the Netherlands Film Production Incentive, the Flanders Audiovisual Fund (VAF), CoBO, the Belgian Tax Shelter, Eurimages and RTL Film LLC. Paradiso Filmed Entertainment expects to release the film in the Benelux next year. S.S. title: Caleb Landry Jones on the Five-Year Battle to Make ‘Down the Arm of God,’ Confronting Prejudices Against Homelessness and How Luc Besson Saved the Film
full_text: Aug 11, 2026 11:31pm PT Caleb Landry Jones on the Five-Year Battle to Make ‘Down the Arm of God,’ Confronting Prejudices Against Homelessness and How Luc Besson Saved the Film The film will world premiere at the Locarno Film Festival on Aug. 12. By Matt Minton Plus Icon Matt Minton mminton@variety.com Latest ‘Assassin’s Creed’ Creator’s New Action-Adventure Game ‘1666: Amsterdam’ Sets Early Access Release (Gaming News Roundup) 12 hours ago How Vera Drew, Louise Weard and More Trans and Nonbinary Filmmakers Are Taking Control of Their Stories Outside the Studio System: ‘We’re Creating a New Industry’ 13 hours ago ‘Josephine’ Trailer: Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan Star as Struggling Parents in Sundance Award-Winning Psychological Thriller 19 hours ago See All Caleb Landry Jones in 'Down the Arm of God' Trying to find funding for “ Down the Arm of God ” proved to be a difficult five-year ordeal for lead star and co-writer Caleb Landry Jones — one that brought the “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri” and “Get Out” actor to terms with the very real-world prejudices that his film grapples with. “Some people were worried about any kind of re-enactment of anyone’s past. We were getting a lot of folks that felt what we were trying to do was not respectful, that we were getting into possible problems of white saviorism,” Jones tells Variety of the decision to cast real homeless people in Texas. “Other things would be simply that the cast wasn’t big enough. That my name isn’t big enough. ‘We need two or three other cast members that are stars!'” Related Stories ‘The Secret Agent’ Star Maria Fernanda Cândido to Lead ‘Lost Objects’ by Brazilian Director Luiz Fernando Carvalho (EXCLUSIVE) Julie Andrews Turned Down 'Princess Diaries 3' Offer Because 'I Think I'm Retired' From On-Screen Acting: 'They Asked Me All Last Year' If I'd Return When “Leon” director Luc Besson saw how much Jones was struggling to secure funding while working with him on the 2025 horror film “Dracula,” he decided to step in with funds and, essentially, save the film under his EuropaCorp producing banner. Now, “Down the Arm of God” will have its world premiere at the Locarno Film Festival in Switzerland on Aug. 12. Popular on Variety Helmed by Peter Brunner, who directed Jones in 2018’s “To the Night,” Jones leads the cast as Nick, a pastor set on making a change when he arrives in a small Texas town and sees the homeless epidemic quietly happening in everyone’s backyard. However, he is swiftly met with pushback from the local community, especially after Nick invites the homeless encampment to sleep inside their church during the harsh winter. The pushback eventually escalates to violence, leading Nick to confront his connection to God. Jones says there were times when he questioned Nick’s earnestness: “I like the ambiguity and these aspects of the character. This was Peter’s choice from the beginning.” The film, which is based in part on true events, started simply as a story of forgiveness between father and son. The estranged father-son dynamic remains central, as Nick feels called to action after struggling to help his father, who is suffering from poverty. That framework eventually became a vehicle to work with the homeless community “without forcing any language down anybody’s throats,” Jones says. As Brunner and Jones began digging into research over the course of five years and meeting with nonprofit organizations across Dallas, Austin and Amarillo, they kept hearing the same note: “We couldn’t make this film with actors, that we’d be doing a disservice to portray homelessness in our country,” Jones says. That note was also echoed by the homeless people that Brunner and Jones, who penned the screenplay together, spoke to. Over the course of five years, many of the homeless people who agreed to be part of “Down the Arm of God” died before production could begin. “The film is, in a big way, dedicated to those people as well,” Jones says. The violence that the film builds to — with protestors in the conservative, homogeneous Texas community holding “White Lives Matter” signs directed at the people of color in the homeless encampment — is another way Jones and Brunner aimed to directly reflect reality. “Everything is there because it felt like if it wasn’t there, we were negating it,” Jones says. Jones commends many of the homeless people who made their on-screen debut and tapped into their own personal experiences. “The work itself wasn’t easy, but to do the work was very easy. Some of the best actors I’ve ever worked with were on this film because it really was on the line of — it wasn’t really acting sometimes, and sometimes it was rooted in a memory. It’s a real memory that the person is speaking of. Sometimes it is fabricated, especially for myself and my character. I am not a pastor, and my father is not homeless … A lot of things. I’m the outlier in the group,” Jones says. “What was difficult were the logistics and trying to get people to understand the severity of homelessness.” As the film nears its festival debut, Jones hopes the film will make audiences across the world reckon with how close everyone is to the poverty line — especially as the homeless epidemic only gets “worse.” “It’s something that most of us deny ourselves all the time, that we are far removed because we have this job. We have these things in our life that we see as steady,” Jones says. “I think COVID woke a lot of people up financially and seeing the repercussions of so many jobs disappearing at once, but I don’t think we really woke up to the fact that it could be us.” Lela Rochon on the Final Season of ‘The Chi,’ the Beauty of Nostalgia and Pushing for More Women-Led Stories Paramount+, Starz, MGM+ and More Are Down to $1/Month With These Early Prime Day Video Deals ‘Murder of JonBenét Ramsey’ Limited Series Moves to Netflix From Paramount+ ‘Crutch’ Canceled After One Season at Paramount+ ‘Clueless’ Sequel Series With Alicia Silverstone Ordered at Paramount+ ‘Criminal Minds’ Star Paget Brewster Tells TV Journalist to ‘Work at a Shelter’ After Mixed Review, Sparking Outrage From Other Critics Loading comments... title: Makeup Oscar Record Holder Recalls Turning Jim Carrey Into the Grinch, Transforming Michael Jackson for ‘Thriller’ and Playing King Kong
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 11, 2026 11:00pm Rick Baker plus monsters Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival The 79 th edition of the Locarno Film Festival will have Oscar royalty in the house on Wednesday evening – well, on its big 8,000-seat square, the Piazza Grande, to be precise. It will bestow its Vision Award, presented by Ticinomoda, upon Rick Baker , a seven-time Oscar winner, a record in the makeup and hairstyling field, and the creator behind some of cinema’s most fantastical creatures. While at the Swiss festival, Baker is also presenting two key films from his career, namely An American Werewolf in London (1981) and The Nutty Professor (1996). The former marked his first Oscar win in 1981, followed by Harry and the Hendersons (1987), Ed Wood (1994), The Nutty Professor (1996), Men in Black (1997), How the Grinch Stole Christmas (2000) and The Wolfman (2010). Related Stories Movies Crunchyroll, Sony Nab Makoto Shinkai's Untitled Next Anime Film for Global Release Lifestyle How Julie Andrews' Singing Poodle Inspired New Children's Book With Daughter You also know Baker’s work from Michael Jackson ‘s famous Thriller video, in which he also played an on-screen role. “From his early make-up work on genre films in the 1970s to his sophisticated creature and character designs for large-scale studio productions, Rick Baker has forged a new visual grammar for cinematic metamorphosis, earning him a record number of Academy Awards for best makeup and cementing his status as a reference point for generations of artists,” said Locarno organizers when they first unveiled his honor. “Rick Baker was responsible for a Copernican revolution in cinema: visionary and revolutionary, he opened new paths for the imagination of entire generations, showing what it truly means to witness physical transmutation on the big screen,” highlighted Locarno artistic director Giona A. Nazzaro . “His filmography includes collaborations with George Lucas and David Cronenberg, Brian De Palma and Joe Dante, Tim Burton and Peter Jackson, John Carpenter and Mike Nichols, among many others.” Before arriving in Locarno for his festival honor, Baker, 75, talked to THR about some of his best-known creations and some of the wacky experiences he had during his career. Why did you end up wanting to work in the fields of makeup and transforming the look of actors and other performers? I grew up in front of the TV. It was that first generation of kids to grow up in front of a TV. I loved those monster movies, and I loved the makeups. In Frankenstein , Boris Karloff just blew me away. Before I realized that makeup artist was what I wanted to be, I used to think I wanted to be a doctor because I wanted to be Doctor Frankenstein. I wanted to be a doctor, and I was going to have a basement laboratory, and I was going to make monsters. But then I grew up a little bit and also found out that I’m extremely squeamish – I don’t like the sight of real blood. Also, my dad was kind of a ham. He’s actually in Schlock . In the first of the banana murders, there’s a dead guy on the ground. That’s my dad. But [director and star] John Landis redubbed his voice with his own voice. How did you go about creating the look of a character, especially since you would work with all these made-up characters, such as the Grinch? Does the personality of the actors play into how you create a look at all? When I got a call from Brian Grazer, who said, “We’re going to do How the Grinch Stole Christmas , and we want Jim Carrey to be the Grinch.” I thought that’s great because Jim can make a lot of faces. I almost immediately visualized what it ended up being. So that was all smooth sailing? Well, the studio kept saying, “We just want Jim to be painted green.” And I went, “No, that’s going to ruin the movie.” You know, it’s not called How the Green Jim Carrey Stole Christmas . It’s the Grinch, so he should be this recognizable character. It is hard turning a 2D drawing into something. But I took what I could from that and added some Rick Baker to it. But to convince them to go with what I thought was the right way, I did the makeup on myself, filmed it and sent it to them. They went: “Well, it doesn’t look like Jim Carrey!” And I said: ‘Well, it will look more like Jim when it’s on Jim.” I mean, our face is very different. You’re not paying him for the look but for his acting, and he’s going to make this thing a really cool character. We prepared for 10 different tests – from painting Jim Carrey green to what we eventually ended up with. I eventually felt I had to save these guys from themselves and from making a wrong decision here. I contacted Ain’t It Cool News , and they wrote a post along the lines of: “Rick Baker did this really cool makeup on himself as the Grinch, and Universal wants to paint Jim Carrey green.” And there were thousands of responses. So, two weeks before filming, they decided, okay, we’ll go for it. Was there any other challenge with the Grinch movie? Actually, the bigger problem I saw was the Whos, the people in Whoville. In the book, they look almost like insect people, which is going to be too weird. And as Cindy Lou Who, they cast a six-year-old Taylor Momsen. And I said: We can’t put a little girl into a three-hour makeup [session]. So we came up with a whole way that we thought it would all work. I rationalized a lot on the Whos, saying: When they’re little, their nose is more human-like, but as they grow, it moves up their face. So we could just paint her nose a little different color and give her these big teeth and give Cindy the long eyelashes. Now, she’s a kick-ass rock star. I don’t know if you know. She’s in a band called The Pretty Reckless as the lead singer. She opens for AC/DC. She opened for the [Rolling] Stones. She’s really great. She’s got an incredible voice, and we became friends because I had daughters of the same age, and my daughters are in the Grinch movie too in a couple of scenes. How did you come up with the ideas for Michael Jackson’s Thriller ? Thriller wasn’t as hard as a lot of other things I’ve done. It was kind of a no-brainer. I had done zombies before. Michael saw American Werewolf , and that’s why he hired John [Landis] as the director. He wanted to transform into a werewolf. Personally, I didn’t think he should be a werewolf. I thought he was much more feline. So I suggested we make him a werecat. I just thought the feline structure fit him much better. The thing with Thriller was that we had no time and very little money on my end, and it was really just me working my butt off for weeks. Also, the dancers weren’t cast until the very end, and I said to John: “I can’t do what I normally do in a few days with this many people. Normally, we’d take a live mask of the people, sculpt custom appliances for them, mold them, cast them.” So, he suggested a different solution: “I said I think what I can do is make some generic pieces that really are just in this area of a bandit mask, so you don’t have to deal with the proportions of the nose. We could make big teeth that we could put in them with some denture-like material, but I said that’s not going to be cool enough. So I said we should have featured zombies that are much cooler than the others. My crew and I all had our life casts already. I also had my body cast. So we started doing very cool zombies that we knew would be much more exciting than the dancer zombies. So, I’m in Thriller . My whole crew is also in Thriller . I am the bearded zombie who opens the crypt with my eyes rolled up. Does it help with your makeup choices that you have put makeup on yourself? I think it’s important. I think a makeup artist should have been made up, so they know what it’s like on the inside. And beyond your cameo in Thriller , you have acted a few more times, right? Yes, I played King Kong in the 1976 King Kong , directed by Federico De Laurentiis and produced by [his father] De Laurentiis, for which I made the suit. And I was determined not to be a whiny, complaining actor in that, like some people are when you put makeup on them. I didn’t have a dressing room. So, I would have to take my street clothes off on the stage and put this bear hide suit on and then sit there and sweat my brains out. I read that you stepped in to play King Kong late in the process and that there was some debate about whether to use your gorilla suit or another one? When I was younger, all the information I had about what a gorilla was came from movies, especially the original King Kong , and from any movies in the ’40s. I felt a gorilla was a real-life monster, and I started looking at films with gorilla suits in it and finding books and National Geographics and other things with gorillas in them. When I was younger, I thought I could make a realistic gorilla costume and fool people with it. So I was set on that path. The problem was I grew up very lower-middle-class. So to make a gorilla suit was a really hard thing, but I figured out ways to do it on a budget. Years later, John Landis and I had become friends, and one day he goes, “Hey, did you hear some Italian guy is going to remake King Kong ?” Somehow they got my number and knew that I had made a gorilla costume, and I thought this would be my only opportunity to really have a budget and make a real gorilla suit. This was in the era of disaster movies, and Kong was just another disaster. And they wanted to make him more like a primitive man. I was 25 years old and went in there. I don’t have a filter. So, I brought in these mechanical gorilla hand extensions so you could have longer arms. They said: “We don’t need that shit. It’s going to be more man-like.” I thought these guys were fucking crazy. If anything, it should be a super gorilla. It should not be less of a gorilla. Kong is the greatest gorilla ever. They would rag on the original movie, and I just said: “You’ll be lucky if you can make anything near that film.” But I was still interested, and I thought I could convince them to change their mind. But I didn’t hear from them, so I took another film. And as soon as I took the other film, they called me and said, “Yes, we want you to do this.” So I told them I needed six weeks to complete this other thing. When I came back, in the meantime, Dino had hired his friend from Italy, Carlo Rombaldi. They said he was a genius and wanted us to work together. But he didn’t speak English, and I don’t speak Italian. How’s that going to work? And it’s not a good thing to have two bosses. They wanted us both to make a test suit; we had six weeks. I think I had something like $10,000, which to me was a lot of money back then, so by myself, basically in my garage, I threw away the drawings they gave me, and I made a gorilla suit. I showed up on the day with my suit, and they were furious. “This looks nothing like what the drawings we gave you. What the hell?” Carlo didn’t have enough time to get the suit done, but he convinced them he could make a 40-foot robot that would do the whole movie. I thought he was delusional. But they wanted to do some tests, and they only had my suit and me. It fit me, so they, regrettably, were using me as King Kong for the test. But they started to get used to me and the costume and look of the suit. A month later or more, Carlo got his suit done, and it was much more like the drawings they gave us, but it was a disaster. For example, my suit had a mechanism where I could control the mouth with my own jaw movements. His suit didn’t have any such mechanism. And John Guillerman, the director, said, “Rick, put your suit on.” And he looked at Carlo’s suit and me. And then he was pointing at mine and said, “Yeah, this is better.” So they picked mine. From there, it was a team effort, but I designed it. And I played King Kong, but the publicity was about a giant robot, so they didn’t want anybody to know that it was this 25-year-old kid in a gorilla costume. You are retired, but do you still do any acting or so? I have done a few things, but just for friends, mostly. My wife and I are in the latest Anthrax video. I don’t know if you’re familiar with Anthrax. The name of the song is “The Edge of Perfection,” and my wife plays my magician’s assistant. The video was directed by Joel Harlow, who’s a makeup artist that I had work with. He’s one of the new makeup artists who do some great stuff. And it’s fun for me. I like dressing up and being somebody else. THR

title: Hansal Mehta, Siddharth Bodke on ‘Scam 2010’ as First Look Unveiled for SonyLIV Series: ‘A Story About Ambition, Influence and Arrogance’ (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Aug 11, 2026 11:00pm PT Hansal Mehta, Siddharth Bodke on ‘Scam 2010’ as First Look Unveiled for SonyLIV Series: ‘A Story About Ambition, Influence and Arrogance’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘SNL U.K.’ Season 2 Sets September Date 17 minutes ago ‘In Flames’ Director Zarrar Kahn Returns to Toronto With Gym-Incel Rom-Com ‘The Lion Does Not Concern Himself,’ Trailer Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE) 30 minutes ago Hansal Mehta, Siddharth Bodke on ‘Scam 2010’ as First Look Unveiled for SonyLIV Series: ‘A Story About Ambition, Influence and Arrogance’ (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago See All SonyLIV/Applause Entertainment Siddharth Bodke’s first look as the lead of “ Scam 2010 ” is out, with director Hansal Mehta and the actor both weighing in on the Birla Studios and Applause Entertainment production for SonyLIV . Based on the book “Sahara: the Untold Story” by Tamal Bandyopadhyay, the series will tell the story of businessman Subrata Roy of the Sahara India Pariwar that operates in the financial services, construction, real estate, sports, manufacturing, hospitality, media and life insurance sectors. In the early 2000s, Roy was accused of several financial misdemeanors, leading to his arrest in 2014. He died in 2023. Related Stories Goya-Nominated Zoe Bonafonte Leads Spain-Argentina Soccer Pioneer Drama ‘Veleta’ (EXCLUSIVE) Rosario Dawson Says Her ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Cameo 'Got Cut Out' and Her Mom Told Her 'That Sucks': ‘I Hope I Get to Be Claire Again’ The show had drawn a legal challenge from Sahara India Pariwar following its announcement in May 2025. Asked by Variety whether the dispute had been resolved, Gaurav Banerjee, managing director and CEO of Sony Pictures Networks India, said, “I believe so.” Popular on Variety “Scam 2010” is the third in a franchise about Indian financial scandals that began with “Scam 1992: The Harshad Mehta Story” and “Scam 2003: The Telgi Story.” Mehta, who directed the original “Scam 1992” and returns for this installment, said: “‘Scam 2010’ is a story about ambition, influence and the arrogance that follows both. It looks at how one of India’s largest business empires was built on belief – and what happened when that belief ran out. It tells the fascinating story of the rise of an empire and the man who mistook it for invincibility.” Bodke, who steps into the lead role, added: “What floored me was the complexity of the lead’s personality and the scale of the show. His passion, power, flaws, rise and eventual downfall make him an incredibly fascinating character to portray. The experience has been nothing short of thrilling for me, and I have relished the opportunity to play such a layered character under the guidance of someone like Hansal Mehta.” Deepak Segal, chief content officer at Applause Entertainment, said: “‘Scam’ has become much more than a franchise for us. ‘Scam 1992’ arrived at a time when the Indian streaming ecosystem was still finding its voice and went on to become one of the most loved and culturally resonant series to emerge from India. title: Crunchyroll, Sony Nab Makoto Shinkai’s Untitled Next Anime Film for Global Release
full_text: × Skip to main content By Patrick Brzeski Plus Icon Patrick Brzeski Asia Bureau Chief View All August 11, 2026 9:51pm Japanese director Makoto Shinkai. MARTIN BUREAU/AFP/ Getty Images Logo text Sony’s Crunchyroll has snapped up global distribution rights to anime hitmaker Makoto Shinkai ‘s much-anticipated next feature. The anime streamer will co-distribute the untitled project with Sony Pictures Entertainment across the world excluding Asia — with the exception of India, which is grouped with the Western territories. Crunchyroll said Tuesday that the film’s title, plot details and expected timing are all being kept under wraps for now. While exceedingly little about the new feature is known, Shinkai is unmistakably one of anime’s biggest blockbuster names. His breakthrough feature Your Name grossed $358 million worldwide in 2016, a landmark in anime’s international expansion. Weathering With You followed in 2019 with $193 million, and 2022’s Suzume took roughly $323 million. All three features rank high among the top-grossing anime films of all time. Related Stories Lifestyle How Julie Andrews' Singing Poodle Inspired New Children's Book With Daughter Movies Why Julie Andrews Won't Return for 'Princess Diaries 3' The new film will follow the same distribution path as Suzume , which was handled jointly by Crunchyroll and Sony Pictures. The film bowed in competition at the Berlin International Film Festival and went on to earn a Golden Globe nomination for best animated feature after earning more than $10 million in U.S. theaters. Shinkai, 53, has released a feature roughly every three years — Your Name in 2016, Weathering With You in 2019, Suzume in 2022 — and anticipation has been building among anime fandom over the past four years about what his next work might be. The director broke his silence in a New Year’s social media message in January, writing that he would finally be able to share concrete details about his next film sometime this year. For Crunchyroll, the deal extends a theatrical run that has made the Sony-owned company the dominant Western distributor of Japanese animation — it claims 12 of the 20 top-grossing anime releases in U.S. history, including Demon Slayer: Infinity Castle , last year’s global phenomenon. title: Paramount Has Spent 100 Years in Hollywood. David Ellison Loved That. Until He Didn’t
full_text: × Skip to main content By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All August 11, 2026 6:18pm Paramount Studios in February. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images “Paramount has deep roots in Southern California. My vision is to stay true to our roots,” wrote David Ellison in a letter to lawmakers representing the state in February. What a difference a few months makes. Now the mogul is locked in a protracted legal battle with the attorneys general of California and 11 other states as he attempts to consummate a $111 billion mega-merger with Warner Bros. Discovery. And he’s in a race against time before a ticking fee penalty of $7 million a day kicks in at the start of October if the deal isn’t done. And each week, it seems, there’s a new leak suggesting the Paramount CEO may be exploring other options to move his company’s headquarters — and taking the idea seriously. On Monday, it was Puck that kicked off another cycle when reporting that Ellison told staffers in a senior leadership meeting he plans to move the company headquarters out of state if the antitrust suit isn’t settled by Oct. 1, when that penalty fee begins. This leak underscores that urgent timetable and could be seen as both a negotiating tactic and a real consideration to pull up anchor for new shores. As The Hollywood Reporter reported in July, Tennessee has been one of the states courting Paramount. Now add Texas, Georgia or another state to the list. The insinuation is that even if the merger eventually goes through, the two historic Hollywood studios could (theoretically) be moving out of their historic homes. So the notion that Ellison would abandon Paramount’s historic place in Hollywood (literally: Paramount’s 65-acre lot, parts of it a century old, is the only big studio in the neighborhood, after all) to finalize his mega-merger isn’t a new one. But this narrative also represents a notable change in tune from Ellison, a California native himself and the product of two California universities, who not long ago was courting state politicians to win their approval for his mega-transaction. In the same letter where he laid out his vision for Paramount staying “true to our roots,” he pointed out that it was his regime that relocated the company’s headquarters from New York to the Paramount studio lot in L.A. Paramount also made a commitment to produce more movies for theatrical release, “all of which means more activity in Hollywood and local jobs,” he claimed. The letter was sent to lawmakers Sen. Adam Schiff and Rep. Laura Friedman in response to their concerns about what the merger would mean for jobs in the state. “Our pledge to continue to license Paramount and Warner Bros. film and shows means there will be additional opportunities available for creative talent in Los Angeles,” Ellison continued. “Our pledge to continue to be active buyers of content from third-party studios and independent producers also means more good-paying jobs in Los Angeles.” For the politicians who received that February letter, the threat to leave the state is prompting a bit of whiplash. “The reason Paramount has been an entertainment powerhouse for over a century is the crews, the writers, the artists, and the local businesses in my district. They are the best in the world at what they do,” said Friedman in a statement to THR . “It would be a massive mistake for Paramount to leave them behind, and it’s wrong to treat the workforce that built Paramount as a bargaining chip in a legal matter.” In his own statement, Schiff said his “north star” was to “protect the jobs of the hardworking Californians” in entertainment. “I hope that Paramount will stick to their commitments to build a stronger Hollywood and keep production here,” he added. And Ellison isn’t the only one at Paramount to have paid lip service to the virtues of working in California. Two of Paramount+’s major upcoming new shows, the Clueless sequel starring Alicia Silverstone and the original series Ascent starring Viola Davis, are filming in L.A. They’re joining other series under the Paramount corporate umbrella, like Matlock , Tracker and NCIS: Origins , that already shoot in the state. As a result, Paramount landed more than $37 million in the last round of California film and television tax credits. “We’re proud to continue investing in the local creative community and production talent who bring our stories to life,” said CBS Studios president David Stapf in a statement on Monday, before the latest reports of Paramount’s roving eyes emerged. How real is the threat to flee the state, then, or is this a laughable pressure tactic? As THR has previously reported , it’s not impossible to imagine Ellison relocating the company headquarters, but the rubber would meet the road on attempting to persuade executives to move their studio work to, say, Nashville or Austin or Atlanta. All told, about 17 percent of the Paramount’s workforce is based in L.A. alone, according to a study from CVL Economics, while 13 percent of Warner Bros. Discovery is based in the area. Good luck to those Paramount execs trying to meet an up-and-coming writer-creator for a casual coffee on Music Row or convincing anyone major other than Taylor Sheridan (who is soon to bid goodbye to the studio anyway) to briefly pop by for a meeting in Texas. That’s not to mention the significant ill will that would be produced by kicking a local industry while it’s down, all while Ellison’s representatives have been presenting him for some time as the savior of Hollywood and its jobs, if only his deal goes through. (“We will continue to fight against any attempt to derail a deal that plainly benefits consumers, creators, and the industry as a whole,” a Paramount spokesperson said in response to a town hall where Hollywood workers aired concerns about job loss as a result of the mega-merger.) The production downturn in California has been so severe that it’s created a grassroots movement to improve production conditions and become a major campaign narrative for L.A.’s mayoral candidates. “Paramount has been an iconic part of Los Angeles for more than a century, and we will work to ensure that Paramount remains rooted in Los Angeles, continues to invest in our city, and continues to support good-paying jobs for Angelenos,” Mayor Karen Bass, who is running for re-election, said in a statement to THR about the company’s latest rattle of the chains. It’s become a marketing tactic for television series and films to flaunt that they were made locally, rather than in, say, Romania or Australia. For now, Ellison is attempting to ward off a trial with a stick, rather than a carrot, but the message keeps shifting. Maybe we should take his word for it that he means business on leaving California. But he said the opposite not too long ago. Aug. 11, 8:48 p.m. Added a statement from L.A. Mayor Karen Bass. THR

title: ‘The Brink of War’ Review: Jeff Daniels Makes an Unpersuasive Ronald Reagan in Talky Historical Drama About Nuclear Summit With Gorbachev
full_text: × Skip to main content By Frank Scheck Plus Icon Frank Scheck View All August 11, 2026 6:00pm Jared Harris (left) and Jeff Daniels in 'The Brink of War.' Courtesy of Angel You have to acknowledge the good intentions behind Michael Russell Gunn’s feature directorial debut depicting the 1986 meeting between Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev in Reykjavik that helped advance the cause of a nuclear reduction treaty. In the film’s press notes, the writer-director emphasizes that his intention was not to make his movie overly political, but rather to illustrate the vital importance of people with different ideologies simply talking with each other in order to bridge divides. To that end, The Brink of War features lots and lots of…talk. That’s not necessarily a bad thing, even though the nearly one-location setting, with lengthy scenes in which the two figures engage in vigorous debate, indicates that the material might have been better served as a play. But then you wouldn’t have had the endless shots of the stunningly beautiful Icelandic landscape that provide visual palette cleansers between the claustrophobic sequences. Related Stories Movies Aisling Bea Joins Brendan Fraser, Jeff Daniels in Sci-Fi Thriller 'Starman' (Exclusive) Movies Jeff Daniels Transforms Into Ronald Reagan in 'Brink of War' Trailer as Angel Studios Hits CinemaCon The Brink of War The Bottom Line History come to only intermittent life. Release date: Friday, August 14 Cast: Jeff Daniels, Jared Harris, Hope Davis, Branka Katic, J.K. Simmons, Aya Cash, Guy Burnet Director-screenwriter: Michael Russell Gunn Rated PG, 1 hour 57 minutes The film concerns an important historical event, in which the world leaders met at a small, rustic and supposedly haunted house at the edge of the sea to discuss their mutual interest in not blowing up the world. The production achieved a coup by filming at the actual location, with the scenes of Reagan ( Jeff Daniels ) and Gorbachev ( Jared Harris ) shot in the room where the meetings took place. The problem is that the filmmaker, who served as a story editor for Aaron Sorkin’s HBO series The Newsroom , is, like his mentor, often too concerned with telling us exactly how to think. Time and time again throughout The Brink of War , the characters expound on the vital importance of their mission and the world-changing stakes involved. The dialogue feels more like speechifying, with such familiar phrases as “Trust but verify” and “Peace through strength” invoked like a band performing its greatest hits in concert. When a frustrated Reagan finally bellows, “Tear down this wall between us, Mr. Gorbachev!” you have to resist the urge to shine your cell phone flashlight. Being superficially familiar with the events in question but not enough of an expert, I can’t vouch for the accuracy of the film’s depiction. Obvious liberties are taken for the sake of cinematic convenience, such as Reagan and Gorbachev talking to each other in English even though they actually spoke via translators. That’s not a problem, although you’d think that in the scenes featuring just Gorbachev and his wily wife Raisa (a scene-stealing Branka Katic) that they would speak in Russian. The lengthy dialogue exchanges between the two main characters are reasonably compelling, even if the slowly-paced film feels longer than its two hours. Much of the credit goes to Harris, who delivers a superb performance as the Soviet leader who desperately wants to achieve an historic agreement but is unwilling to sacrifice his country’s security by allowing Reagan to fulfill his quixotic goal of creating a missile defense shield. When Gorbachev rebukes Reagan about the U.S. not sharing the technology for cow milking machines that would help feed his people, Harris makes the leader’s anger feel fully real. Daniels has a more difficult task, since we’re so much more familiar with Reagan’s looks and voice. Though he’s boasting a mild hair-and-make-up job and the occasional verbal tic of starting a sentence with “Well…” the actor doesn’t deliver a true impression as much as he strives to convey Reagan’s essence. He does a creditable job, but sorry, he looks and sounds so much like Jeff Daniels that it’s hard to buy into the illusion. It’s also hard to be convinced by the film’s depiction of Reagan — whose mental decline may well have begun by that time — as playing sophisticated 4D chess in his negotiations stressing human rights. According to the film, the success of the summit would be determined by Gorbachev’s decision whether or not to let the sister of cellist Mstislav Rostropovich leave Russia to visit him for his birthday. Hope Davis shows up briefly as Nancy Reagan, chafing at being left home in Washington while Raisa Gorbachev flaunts her presence in Iceland to the press, and a not very interesting subplot revolves around two reporters ( Aya Cash , Guy Burnet) covering Raisa throughout the weekend. The ever-reliable J.K. Simmons makes a strong impression as Secretary of State George Shultz, depicted as a voice of reason and to whom the film is dedicated. The film employs a few stylistic devices to alleviate the visual monotony, such as occasional split screens enclosing the two central figures and, in a more heavy-handed example, making the table between them smaller and smaller in different shots to emphasize their diplomatic progress. But the visual touches aren’t enough to prevent The Brink of War from feeling like an academic history lesson rather than living, breathing drama. Hunt, Shannon Laning, Carl Beyer, Dylan Tarason Director of photography: Magdalena Gorka Production designer: Gunnar Palsson Editors: Mike Sale, Laura Yanovich Composer: Austin Wintory Costume designer: Jo Katsaras Casting: Sheila Jaffe, Bryan Reilly Rated PG, 1 hour 57 minutes THR

title: Paramount’s Makan Delrahim Says “Everything Is On The Table” In Finding Merger Resolution, Says Leaving California Is A Consideration But Not “Blackmail”
full_text: Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Paramount’s Makan Delrahim Says “Everything Is On The Table” In Finding Merger Resolution, Says Leaving California Is A Consideration But Not “Blackmail” Kennedy Center Ordered To Pay Jazz Musician Chuck Redd More Than $250,000 In Legal Dispute Over His Opposition To Trump Renaming Tammy Fine To Lead Talent Development For NBC News View All August 11, 2026 5:50pm Screenshot Paramount ‘s Chief Legal Officer Makan Delrahim said that “everything is on the table” when it comes to finding a resolution to a state attorneys general lawsuit seeking to block the company’s proposed merger with Warner Bros. Discovery . At a Politico conference on Tuesday, Delrahim also defended the company’s consideration of exiting California. California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who is leading the state AGs lawsuit and appeared at the same conference hours earlier, called the threat to leave a form of “blackmail.” “David Ellison was born here, lived here since I moved to this country. I’ve lived here. He’s raising his children here. His intent is to be committed to be in California,” Delrahim said. He added, “There’s a point at which where you have a duty, a fiduciary duty to your shareholders, and those are all the factors you consider. But our goal is to be here.” Related Stories News 'Harry Potter' TV Series Due To Hit HBO In 2027: Everything We Know About The Cast, Who's Creating It, What J.K. Rowling Says & More Legal California AG Rob Bonta Open To Structural Remedies In Paramount-WBD Suit But Calls 30 Movies A Year An "Old, Stale Promise" Delrahim said, “I heard the attorney general say that this was some kind of blackmail attempt for the lawsuit. It is not. When the delay starts costing you know after this merger has been approved from, I believe, 67 countries — European Union, China. Canada, Australia — let’s forget about the DOJ — but all of them have reviewed it this way. But this state seems to view this merger in a different market. You have to take a look at the business environment and look to see what’s best for not only the community, the business, and ultimately, go to the place where you are wanted.” Watch on Deadline Ellison told a group of the company’s executives that he would start the process of leaving the state around Oct. 1 if Bonta did not negotiate a settlement. Paramount faces paying a $7 million-per-day ticking fee to Warner Bros. Discovery for each day that the merger doesn’t close past Sept. 30. But a federal judge last week set the trial for next March, scuttling the company’s plans to close the deal as soon as this summer. California and 11 other states sued to block the merger last month, claiming that it would stifle competition for wide release theatrical film distribution, anticipated big budget blockbusters, and basic cable television channel licensing. With the prospect of a trial delaying the transaction well into next year, Paramount has waged a PR campaign to try to show that the deal has drawn industry support, while Ellison has tried to peg the state AG opposition as about concerns over what would happen to CNN, amid warnings that he would push the network in a Trump-friendlier direction. In a new York Times op ed, Ellison wrote that news organizations require independence, while he said that CNN and CBS News, which Paramount already owns, “are here to tell it straight down the middle.” Delrahim pointed to the Ellison op ed, and said that when it came to CNN, the CEO “wants to bring it back to news.” Bonta, though, denied that the lawsuit was about control of the network, and a mere divestment of the channel would not be a sufficient structural remedy to satisfy the state AGs. Delrahim told the Politico conference, “I take [Bonta] at his word. It’s not about CNN.This is an antitrust case. He’s trying to protect movie theaters and cable operators, as alleged in the lawsuit.” But Delrahim predicted that the AGs would not have a viable case at trial. He pointed to support for the merger from major exhibitors, and when it came to the merger’s impact on cable operators, “it will fall apart because of the market definition.” “There is no such thing as basic cable anymore,” he said. “Combined, if you look at streaming, the two companies will have something like 7% to 11% of the market share.” When Politico’s Alex Burns pressed him on the prospect of selling CNN as a way to “make it easier to get this deal done,” Delrahim responded, “I was born in Iran. I moved here after the 1979 revolution. The single most important thing we have is the First Amendment. not because I’m a religious minority and …think people should be free, but also the First Amendment and free speech. If you start using state powers and wrap yourself around that to actually violate the First Amendment and control of content, that would be the saddest day in this country.” He added, “But having said that, everything is on the table. We would be delighted to engage and discuss about any resolution to get this merger, to get this closing after all this time, in order to repair the industry, create more jobs, bring more jobs and production back.” Delrahim also was asked about the prospect that the company would be investigated by Democrats if they take control of one or more chambers of Congress in the midterms. Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-MD), the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, and other Democrats have warned that Paramount would face scrutiny along with other big mergers and efforts to win support from the Trump administration. “You can allege all you want,” Delrahim said. “There is no corruption here.” CEO Threatens To Leave California If Suit Isn’t Settled; AG Calls It “Blackmail” Nicholas Hoult Joins ‘Harry Potter’ As Gilderoy Lockhart For Season 2 ‘Brand New Day’ To Hit $700M U.S. Wednesday; ‘End Of Oak Street’ Due Friday ‘Bourbon & Lies’ Series Based On Books In Works At MGM TV Read More About: 3 Comments

title: Bill Jersey, Two-Time Oscar-Nominated Documentarian, Dies at 99
full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All August 11, 2026 5:48pm Bill Jersey Jerry Telfer/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images Bill Jersey, the Bay Area documentarian who wrote, directed, shot, edited and produced films for more than a half-century, collecting two Oscar nominations and three Emmy noms along the way, has died. He was 99. Jersey died July 24 of congestive heart failure at his home in Lambertville, New Jersey, his wife, Shirley Kessler, told the San Francisco Chronicle . Jersey earned his feature documentary Oscar noms for A Time for Burning (1967), about a white Lutheran minister’s unsuccessful attempt to connect to Black folks in Omaha, Nebraska, and Super Chief: The Life and Legacy of Earl Warren (1990), a profile of the Supreme Court justice that was narrated by Gregory Peck . Related Stories Movies Reggie Bannister, a Horror Icon Known for the 'Phantasm' Franchise, Dies at 80 TV Jon Cypher, Actor in 'Cinderella,' 'Hill Street Blues' and 'Major Dad,' Dies at 94 (As a “culturally, historically or aesthetically significant” work, A Time for Burning was inducted into the Library of Congress’ National Film Registry in 2005.) He also received an International Documentary Association prize and two Emmy noms for his work on the landmark 2002 PBS miniseries The Rise and Fall of Jim Crow , narrated by Richard Roundtree , and created docs about the making of One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest and Amadeus . Jersey made most of his films for Quest Productions, which he launched in 1960 in New York City before relocating in 1981 to Emeryville, California. Starting in 1985, he ran the company out of the Zaentz Media Center in Berkeley, California (the complex also was home to the Fantasy recording studio used by Creedence Clearwater Revival). Several filmmakers, including Gary Meyer, co-founder of the Landmark Theatres chain, had offices there, and Jersey served as a mentor to all for some 40 years. “If a filmmaker wanted feedback, Bill was always there to help them, at all stages of production. If they wanted an honest opinion, they asked Bill,” Meyer told the Chronicle . “Bill helped shape many projects into finished films.” The San Francisco International Film Festival paid tribute to Jersey by screening a selection of his documentaries in 1990. William Clifford Jersey Jr. was born in Queens on June 9, 1927, and raised on Long Island in Port Washington. His father, Clifford, was a bank teller, and his mother, Alice, was a cook in a high school cafeteria. After graduating from Northport Union School in 1945, Jersey served in the U.S. Navy, then attended Houghton College in New York, Wheaton College in Illinois and the USC School of Cinematic Arts, earning his master’s degree in 1957. His first screen credits came as an art director on films including Manhunt in the Jungle and the Steve McQueen-starring The Blob , both released in 1958. After moving back east, Jersey launched Quest and wrote, directed and produced for the anthology series The DuPont Show of the Week , where one 1963 episode, “Manhattan Battleground,” about a Quaker social worker in New York’s Spanish Harlem, got him his first Emmy nom. His credits included Faces of the Enemy (1987), about the psychology of dehumanizing a military adversary; Naked to the Bone (1997), about MRI imaging; Eames: The Architect & the Painter (2011), about the modernist designers Charles and Ray Eames (that doc won a Peabody Award); and American Reds: The Rise and Fall of the American Communist Party (2016). His work tackled such other subjects as Abraham Lincoln, the conflict between creationists and evolutionists, Maya Angelou, organized crime, U.S.‑Soviet relations, the Italian Renaissance and the search for an AIDS vaccine. He also taught at San Francisco State. When he wasn’t making documentaries, Jersey was a landscape painter. After spending his last 18 years on the East Coast, he died in his studio surrounded by his art, his wife said. In addition to Kessler, whom he married in 1985, survivors include his children, Beth, Todd, Brian, Colin and Josh. “If I could use one word to describe my dad, it is ‘big,’” Beth told the Chronicle . “He was larger than life because he would go off and make these amazing films and win all these awards. And he never had a script.” THR

title: WGA Says David Ellison’s Threat That Paramount Will Leave California Over AG’s Antitrust Lawsuit “Proves The Danger Of Its Outsized Power”

title: Doc Talk Podcast: Directors Judd Apatow & Michael Bonfiglio On Their Emmy Contender ‘Mel Brooks: The 99 Year Old Man!’
full_text: Skip to main content By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew Doc Talk Podcast: Directors Judd Apatow & Michael Bonfiglio On Their Emmy Contender ‘Mel Brooks: The 99 Year Old Man!’ ‘Top Of The World’ Trailer: Documentary From Julie Cohen & Betsy West Explores Stunning Restaurant Atop World Trade Center Netflix Acquires ‘An Open Field’ And ‘One Last Order’, Short Docs Primed For Oscar Contention View All August 11, 2026 4:45pm L-R: Judd Apatow and Michael Bonfiglio of 'Mel Brooks: The 99 Year Old Man!' Mark Seliger/ Claudia Woloshin For over 75 years, Mel Brooks has been making people laugh. Hard. He’s brought to the screen Mongo, Lili Von Shtüpp, the grandson of a certain mad scientist (aka Young Frankenstein), Frau Blücher (“A little Ovaltine, perhaps?), Louis XVI (“It’s good to be the king”), Max Bialystock, Leo Bloom, Barf, Dark Helmet, President Skroob, Yogurt, and so many others. The comedy icon, who turned 100 years old on June 28, is the focus of the two-part HBO documentary Mel Brooks: The 99 Year Old Man! (released as he approached the century mark), directed by Emmy winners Judd Apatow and Michael Bonfiglio . It’s got six Primetime Emmy Awards nominations — tied for the most of any nonfiction project — including Outstanding Documentary or Nonfiction Special and Outstanding Directing for a Documentary/Nonfiction Program. Related Stories News Emmy Centenarian Club: David Attenborough Breaks Record For Oldest Nominee, Mel Brooks Doc Earns Recognition Documentary Emmy Contender Judd Apatow On “Piss-Your-Pants” Funny Mel Brooks, His Nikki Glaser Collab, And That Seth Rogen-Anne Hathaway ‘Knocked Up’ Story Apatow and Bonfiglio join the latest edition of Deadline’s Doc Talk podcast to discuss their profile of one of the greatest comedy minds of this or any century (his career really got started in the aughts – the original aughts — two millennia ago as the 2000 Year Old Man). The filmmakers tell us how they got Brooks to drop the veil to allow a glimpse at the man behind the laughs – how Sid Caesar paid Brooks out of his own pocket to write for Your Show of Shows , how he foresaw that his future lay not in TV but in films, his remarkable lifelong friendship with Carl Reiner, and his magnificent love affair with fellow Oscar winner Anne Bancroft. Watch on Deadline Apatow explains how he approached interviews with the legend – and why he feared Mel might yell “cut” at any moment. The writer-director, himself one of comedy’s great talents, explores how Brooks worked around Warner Bros executives who wanted him to dump so many of the best parts of Blazing Saddles before the film’s theatrical release (“Lose Mongo punching the horse,” was just one ill-considered imperative from the exec). Apatow and Bonfiglio also get into how Brooks managed to skewer racism, Nazism and other “isms” without ever losing sight of the key objective – to make it funny. And they opine on who, along with Brooks, belongs on the Mount Rushmore of Comedy – were such a thing to exist. That’s on the new episode of Doc Talk hosted by Oscar winner John Ridley ( 12 Years a Slave, Shirley ) and Matt Carey, Deadline’s senior documentary editor. The pod is a production of Deadline and Ridley’s Nō Studios. Listen to the episode above or on major podcast platforms including Spotify , iHeart and Apple . title: Nicholas Hoult Boards ‘Harry Potter’ Season 2 as Gilderoy Lockhart
full_text: Skip to main content By Rick Porter Plus Icon Rick Porter Television Business Editor rickporter Follow Sign Up View All August 11, 2026 3:31pm Nicholas Hoult Neilson Barnard/Getty Images Logo text HBO ‘s Harry Potter series has locked in a key role for season two. Nicholas Hoult ( Superman, The Great ) has joined the series as Professor Gilderoy Lokckhart, who comes to Hogwarts in Harry’s (Dominic McLaughlin) second year as the new Defense Against the Dark Arts teacher. Lockhart is a key character in Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets , the second book in J.K. Rowling’s series and the source material for season two of the show. The character is renowned in the wizarding world for his many heroic deeds, though he’s later revealed as a fraud who took credit for the acts of others after erasing part of their memories. Kenneth Branagh previously played Lockhart in the 2002 Chamber of Secrets film. The show’s first season, officially titled Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone , is set to premiere Dec. 25. Along with McLaughlin, the show’s core cast includes Arabella Stanton (Hermione Granger), Alastair Stout (Ron Weasley), John Lithgow (Albus Dumbledore), Janet McTeer (Minerva McGonagall), Paapa Essiedu (Severus Snape), Nick Frost (Rubeus Hagrid), Rory Wilmot (Neville Longbottom) and Lox Pratt (Draco Malfoy). Francesca Gardiner is the showrunner for season one and executive produces with Mark Mylod (who also directs multiple episodes); Rowling, Neil Blair, and Ruth Kenley-Letts of Brontë Film and TV; and David Heyman of Heyday Films, who produced the eight Harry Potter movies. Jon Brown ( Succession ) is co-showrunner with Gardiner on season two. Hoult broke out in 2002’s About a Boy opposite Hugh Grant. His credits also include Nosferatu, The Menu and four X-Men movies, starting with 2011’s First Class . He’ll next be seen in Amazon MGM’s How to Rob a Bank and the Disney+/Hulu series Mosquito , from The Great creator Tony McNamara. Hoult is repped by UTA, 42, Sloane Offer and Relevant.
